title: Inside Nagpur's Saoji Cuisine: The 150-Year-Old Tradition Behind India's Spiciest Mutton Curry
excerpt: Born in the kitchens of Halba Koshti weavers who migrated to Nagpur in 1877, Saoji food uses a closely guarded 32-spice masala and is now spreading from central India to Japan.
body:
• Saoji cuisine traces back to the 1870s when the Halba Koshti weavers migrated from Madhya Pradesh to Nagpur after Jamsetji Tata opened the Empress Mills in 1877.
  • The masala uses a blend of 32 spices — including black pepper, cinnamon, cloves, poppy seeds, and roasted coconut — ground fresh and cooked in jute oil, making it one of Maharashtra's spiciest cuisines.
  • From a handful of mill-side food stalls in the mid-1900s, Nagpur now has roughly 500 Saoji restaurants, and advocates are pushing for a Geographical Indication tag to protect the cuisine's authenticity.
  • A Japanese chef named Takashi Takeshima has brought Saoji to Fukuoka, while hotel chefs and home-run businesses are spreading the cuisine to Pune, Mumbai, and beyond.

In the lanes of old Nagpur, a plate of Saoji mutton curry arrives in a shade somewhere between burnt sienna and arterial red. One bite sets off a slow, escalating burn — first the black pepper, then the cinnamon, then the dried red chillies in a 32-spice masala that pulls no punches. Sweat beads on the forehead. Eyes water. And then you take another bite, because that is the whole point.

Saoji cuisine is Nagpur's signature food — a fiercely spiced, predominantly non-vegetarian cooking tradition that has sustained generations of working-class families in Maharashtra's Vidarbha region. It is spicier than the better-known Kolhapuri and Malwani styles, yet remains relatively unknown beyond central India. That is slowly changing.

From Looms to Ladles

The story of Saoji food begins not in a kitchen but on a loom. The Halba Koshti community, a tribal group of handloom weavers from what is now Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, migrated to Nagpur around 1877 when Jamsetji Tata established the Empress Mills textile factory. The weavers settled in large numbers around the mill compounds, bringing with them centuries-old weaving skills and a cooking tradition built on robust, intensely spiced meals that sustained them through long hours of manual work.

"Saoji food goes back to the 1870s. There was a weavers' community called Halba Koshti in Madhya Pradesh. The women of this community created this Saoji masala with a blend of 32 selected spices."

— Chef Amit Chakraborti, Executive Chef, Le Meridien Nagpur

When mechanized textiles undercut handloom work by the mid-20th century, the community pivoted. "As mills closed and markets dwindled, this was the easiest way to earn a living," one community elder recalled, according to The News Dirt. Women, traditionally the custodians of spice-mixing knowledge, led the enterprise. What had been private home recipes turned into a public trade.

The 32-Spice Secret

The foundation of every Saoji dish is a masala of extraordinary complexity. Black pepper, dried coriander, bay leaves, black cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, star anise, poppy seeds, nutmeg, and roasted coconut are among the roughly 32 ingredients that are dry-roasted and ground fresh. The coconut is roasted until nearly black, lending the paste its characteristic dark color. Traditionally, linseed oil — locally called jute oil — is used instead of ghee, producing a distinct earthy aroma.

"The unique blending and balancing of spices makes Saoji food different," second-generation Saoji restaurant owner Ajay Jarulkar told The News Dirt, noting that authentic recipes are still cooked in earthen pots with fresh-pressed oils. The spice formulas are closely guarded family secrets. "The trick lies in mixing the spices, which is known only to Koshti women," says Ramesh Saharkar, whose father started one of the earliest Saoji outlets in the town of Umred.

What makes Saoji stand apart from Maharashtra's other spicy cuisines is the absence of any tangy counterbalance. "Malwani and Kolhapuri spice blends have a slight tanginess to them, which Saoji spice blends don't have," explains Chef Chakraborti. "The tanginess makes those spices less hot. In Saoji masala, there is no tangy ingredient, so the spiciness is not diluted one bit."

500 Restaurants and a GI Tag Push

From the first dedicated Saoji eatery — reportedly opened at Golibar Chowk by a weaver-turned-chef named Mama Dhamarkar in the 1970s — the cuisine has spawned roughly 500 restaurants across Nagpur, according to The Culture Trip. No main road in the city lacks one. The quintessential Saoji thali features mutton or chicken curry alongside zunka, bhakhri, and masale bhaat.

The cuisine also birthed Nagpur's beloved breakfast staple: Tarri Poha. Halba Koshti vendors paired mild poha — flattened rice sautéed with onions and turmeric — with a ladle of tarri, a fiery kala chana curry thick with the signature spice blend. The combination became inseparable from Nagpur's morning routine, spreading from mill gates to college campuses.

Advocates have been pushing for a Geographical Indication tag to protect Saoji cuisine's authenticity, much like champagne or Darjeeling tea, arguing that the growing number of imitators risks diluting the tradition.

Going Global, One Kitchen at a Time

In Fukuoka, Japan, a chef named Takashi Takeshima runs a small kitchen beneath the Midori Store umbrella, serving fiery mutton gravies and phulkas straight from Nagpur's playbook. His story, reported by Homegrown, traces an unlikely path: late-night internet research into Indian recipes drew him to descriptions of a "brazen, brick-red curry," leading to years of studying the cuisine and eventually opening shop in one of Japan's food capitals.

Back in India, entrepreneurs like Pune-based Shilpi Gulati, who runs a weekend Saoji catering business using spices sourced exclusively from Nagpur, are working to introduce the cuisine to new audiences. At Le Meridien Nagpur, Chef Chakraborti serves Saoji chicken croissants alongside traditional thalis to give international visitors an entry point. "I'm sure that Saoji cuisine will be very famous in a few more years," he says. For now, a plate of Saoji mutton remains one of Indian food's best-kept secrets — one that rewards anyone brave enough to handle the heat.

nri_angle: Saoji cuisine connects NRIs from Nagpur and Vidarbha to their regional food identity, while a Japanese chef's embrace of the tradition highlights Indian cuisine's growing global reach.
